analysis.summary:
Your clinical presentation reveals a complex but highly treatable pattern: Liver Qi Stagnation driven by prolonged stress, sitting upon a foundation of Spleen Qi Deficiency, with secondary Damp-Heat inflammation expressed through your skin. The red tongue with teeth marks is diagnostically crucial—the redness indicates active heat inflammation burning in your body, but the teeth marks reveal that your Qi is depleted and cannot effectively contain this heat or circulate it smoothly. Your cool limbs and abdomen confirm this Qi Deficiency with poor lower-body warming. The crimson plaques with migratory itching are classic signs of Wind carrying Damp-Heat through your skin; they spread because your defensive Qi boundary is weakened by the underlying systemic Qi depletion.

The emotional and stress components are not incidental features—they are the engine driving your physical illness. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Liver system governs the smooth, unobstructed flow of Qi and is intimately connected to emotional regulation and stress resilience. When you encounter chronic stress and psychological pressure (as you have over the past year), the Liver becomes constrained, Qi stagnates, and this stagnation generates heat. This heat rises toward your upper body, driving the inflammatory plaques on your face and trunk. Meanwhile, your Spleen—weakened by constitutional factors or acquired depletion—cannot transform and transport Qi effectively, allowing pathogenic Damp-Heat to accumulate in your tissue spaces and express through your skin. The anxiety and inferiority complex are not separate psychiatric symptoms; they are direct manifestations of Liver Qi Stagnation affecting your Heart-Spirit (the center of consciousness and emotional resilience in TCM). The chronic skin inflammation then feeds back into your stress, perpetuating the cycle.

This integrated pattern explains why all your symptoms are interconnected: the anxiety and stress sensitivity reflect Liver system constraint; the red, itchy, migratory plaques reflect Wind-Damp-Heat with weak defensive Qi; the dandruff indicates unresolved dampness at the surface level; the body temperature dysregulation (upper body hot, lower body cool) reflects Yang Qi unable to defend and circulate properly; and the year-long persistence reflects that your Spleen Qi deficiency cannot self-correct without external support. Your condition is fundamentally a disturbance in Qi circulation, stress regulation, and metabolic function—not primarily a dermatological disease requiring topical steroids, though dermatological support may have temporary benefit.

Recovery is entirely achievable with a coordinated, whole-system approach. The treatment strategy will soothe your Liver and restore smooth Qi flow to reduce emotional burden and heat accumulation; tonify your Spleen Qi and restore metabolic function to eliminate the foundation that allows Damp-Heat to accumulate; gently clear the pathogenic Damp-Heat and Wind without further damaging your depleted Qi; and calm your Heart-Spirit to interrupt the stress-inflammation feedback loop. Most patients with similar patterns see significant improvement in 6–8 weeks with consistent herbal support, daily practice of stress-management techniques (meditation, Tai Chi, or gentle yoga), dietary alignment with your pattern, and acupoint self-care. Emotional lightness and reduced anxiety typically precede skin healing by 1–2 weeks, as Qi begins to flow freely again.

key_findings.from_inquiry: One year of crimson plaques with dry itching desquamation on face, trunk, and limbs; itching moves around body (indicates Qi stagnation and Wind component); heavy physical and psychological stress (Liver Qi stagnation driver); feelings of inferiority and low mood (Heart-Spirit disturbance from Liver constraint); limbs and abdomen cooler than normal while upper body runs hot (Qi deficiency with Yang unable to circulate, heat floating upward).
key_findings.from_visual: Tongue rather red (indicates heat inflammation) with prominent teeth marks (indicates Qi deficiency, poor transformation and transportation function). The combination of red with teeth marks is pathognomonic for Qi Deficiency unable to contain heat—a key diagnostic finding in this case.
key_findings.from_pulse: Data incomplete, but clinical pattern strongly suggests a Qi-deficient pulse (likely weak, possibly fine) with an underlying heat component (potentially slightly rapid or wiry if stress/stagnation are pronounced). In Qi Deficiency, the pulse often lacks strength and cannot reach the fingertip fully, reflecting depleted defensive and metabolic function.
key_findings.from_other: No fever mentioned, suggesting interior rather than exterior condition (consistent with chronic one-year course). No mention of thirst or scanty urine (suggesting this is not pure Yin Deficiency Heat), but the teeth marks and cool extremities contradict pure Cold pattern, pointing to mixed Qi-Deficiency-with-Heat pattern.

analysis.pattern_rationale: The diagnosis of Liver Qi Stagnation with Spleen Qi Deficiency and Damp-Heat is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) Psychological stress and one-year duration point to Liver Qi Stagnation as the primary driver; (2) Red tongue with teeth marks is the cardinal finding for Qi Deficiency unable to contain heat, directly pointing to the 'true-deficiency-false-excess' or 'root-deficiency-branch-excess' pattern; (3) Migratory itching and crimson plaques reflect both Wind component and Heat excess, while the spreading nature indicates weak boundary defenses (weak Wei Qi from Qi deficiency); (4) Cool limbs and abdomen despite upper body heat indicate a Yang Qi circulation disorder (Qi Deficiency pattern) with heat floating upward rather than descending; (5) Anxiety and inferiority complex directly point to Liver-Heart disharmony from Liver Qi Stagnation affecting the Spirit; (6) Dandruff indicates unresolved dampness, and the 12-month chronicity reflects that Qi deficiency cannot self-correct (unlike acute excess conditions that may spontaneously resolve). The pattern is consistent with Classical TCM teaching: stress (external trigger) → Liver Qi Stagnation (primary mechanism) → heat generation and upward floating (excess manifestation) + constrained circulation → inadequate Spleen function → Damp-Heat accumulation (secondary excess) + weak Wei Qi boundary → skin inflammation. This is a true example of 虚实夹杂 (mixed deficiency-excess pattern).

treatment.therapeutic_principle: First, course-clear and move Liver Qi to unblock the stagnation and reduce heat generation. Second, tonify Spleen Qi and restore transformation and transportation function to eliminate the damp-heat-accumulation foundation and strengthen the defensive Qi boundary. Third, gently clear pathogenic Damp-Heat and Wind without further depleting Qi (avoid harsh purgatives or cold bitter herbs that would damage Spleen Qi further). Fourth, calm the Heart-Spirit to reduce anxiety and interrupt the stress-inflammation feedback loop. Treatment emphasis shifts from clearing stagnation and excess early on, toward gradual tonification as stagnation resolves.
treatment.treatment_method: Begin with modified Free Constraint Powder (a classical formula addressing Liver Qi stagnation and Spleen Qi deficiency, enhanced with heat-clearing herbs) taken at 6-8g twice daily for 2-4 weeks. As symptoms improve and stagnation clears, gradually increase tonification herbs and reduce clearing herbs. Concurrently, begin daily acupoint self-massage (particularly Liver 3 and Stomach 36 to regulate Liver and support Spleen), commit to daily stress-management practice (meditation, Tai Chi, or gentle yoga for 20-30 minutes), and align diet with the therapeutic direction (tonify Qi, clear Damp-Heat gently, avoid aggravating heat and stress). Expect emotional improvement to precede skin healing; reassess and adjust formula every 3-4 weeks based on symptom evolution. After 6-8 weeks, transition to a maintenance formula if needed or continue with lifestyle management alone.

beneficial: Mung beans (green legume)—cooling in nature, clear Damp-Heat and heat toxins, transform dampness, support spleen qi, excellent for red plaques and heat manifestation

Job's tears (pearl barley, a mild grain)—strengthen spleen, transform dampness, promote healing of chronic inflammation, nourish without generating excess heat, used in skin-healing broths for centuries

White fungus (tremella, a mild fungal food)—nourish Lung Qi and yin without warming, support skin elasticity, gentle cooling action for chronic heat conditions, well-tolerated by Qi-deficient patients
Lily bulb (white, fresh or dried)—calm Heart-Spirit and reduce anxiety, clear heat, moisten lungs, support Yin, excellent for stress-related anxiety paired with heat plaques
Jujube (red date, whole fruit)—tonify Qi gently, calm Spirit, support root deficiency without aggravating heat, used as a harmonizer in most Qi-tonifying broths, sweet and safe long-term
Honey (raw or processed)—tonify Spleen Qi and stomach function, moisten lungs, mild cooling action, supports healing of depleted conditions, a classic Spleen-supporting food
recipes: Spleen-Tonifying Qi Broth: Simmer 1 handful each of Job's tears and white fungus with 3-5 jujubes, 1 small piece of ginger (thin slice), and 5 cups water for 45 minutes until the ingredients are very soft. Drink 1 cup daily, especially in the morning. This tonifies Spleen Qi, calms spirit, and provides mild heat-clearing without aggravating deficiency.

Cooling Mung Bean and Lily Bulb Soup: Soak 1 cup mung beans and 10 dried lily bulb scales overnight. Simmer together with 2 slices ginger and 6 cups water for 90 minutes until mung beans are very soft. Add honey to taste. Drink 1 cup 2-3 times weekly. This is ideal during acute flaring of heat and itching; cooling without being harsh, supports anxiety.

Qi and Spleen Restoration Rice Congee: Cook 1/2 cup white rice with 1 small piece of Ginseng (optional, or use 6 Astragalus slices as substitute if ginseng is too warming), 3-5 jujubes, and 6 cups water very slowly for 2 hours until very creamy. Eat a warm bowl for breakfast 5 days per week. This is the foundational tonification meal for Qi-deficient patients, mild enough for daily use.

foods_to_avoid: Spicy foods (chili, black pepper, hot sauce)—heat the Liver further, aggravate itching and plaques, and feed Qi stagnation and constraint

Alcohol (beer, wine, spirits)—heats the Liver system, exacerbates Qi stagnation, impairs Spleen transformation, and is a known trigger for inflammatory skin conditions; smoking similarly damages Lung Qi and destabilizes skin immunity

Deep-fried and greasy foods (fried chicken, chips, pastries, fatty meat cuts)—create additional dampness, burden the weak Spleen's transformation function, generate Damp-Heat accumulation, and perpetuate plaques

Shellfish and shrimp (except occasional white fish)—warming in nature, potentially damp-heat generating, known trigger for itching and plaques in heat-sensitive skin conditions; white fish is neutral and acceptable

Chocolate, caffeine (coffee, strong tea, energy drinks)—stimulate the nervous system, feed anxiety and Heart-Spirit disturbance, trigger Liver Qi stagnation, and exacerbate itching in stress-sensitive patients
High-sugar and refined carbohydrates (candy, white bread, pastries, soft drinks)—impair Spleen function, generate dampness, and destabilize blood sugar—which amplifies anxiety and stress response
lifestyle: Daily stress management and emotional processing (the most critical intervention): Commit to 20-30 minutes of daily meditation, Tai Chi, Qigong, or gentle yoga. This directly addresses Liver Qi Stagnation by promoting Qi flow, calming the nervous system, and interrupting the stress-anxiety-inflammation cycle. Tai Chi and Qigong are particularly effective because they specifically train smooth, unobstructed Qi circulation, which is the root mechanism you need to restore. If formal practice is difficult, daily walking meditation or even conscious breathing (in-count of 4, hold 4, out-count of 6) during stressful moments provides significant benefit.

Establish a consistent sleep schedule aligned with Liver system healing: Go to bed before 23:00 and rise between 06:00-07:00. The Liver system has a 'peak activity time' between 23:00-03:00, and sleep during this window allows the body to process stress and regulate Qi flow. Irregular sleep actively aggravates Liver Qi Stagnation and prevents healing. A consistent rhythm is more important than total hours.

Avoid overheating and excessive sun exposure: Since your upper body runs hot and you have Damp-Heat skin inflammation, avoid intense exercise in direct heat, avoid saunas, and minimize prolonged heat exposure. Gentle exercise in cool environments or water (swimming in cool pools) is ideal. Evening or early morning exercise is preferable to afternoon heat training.

Practice regular emotional processing and self-compassion: The inferiority complex and anxiety are both consequences of and reinforcers of your Liver Qi Stagnation. Consider journaling (10-15 minutes daily), talking with a trusted friend or counselor, or practicing self-compassion meditation (recognizing that dermatitis does not reflect your character or worth). TCM treatment will reduce the physical inflammation, but emotional work will accelerate the shift in your nervous system response.
acupoints: Liver 3 / Tai Chong (太冲 LV3): Located in the webbing between the first and second metatarsal bones on the dorsum of the foot. Press and massage in small circles with your thumb for 2-3 minutes bilaterally, once or twice daily. This is the source point of the Liver channel and directly regulates Liver Qi flow, reduces stress response, and calms agitation. Essential for this pattern.

Spleen 6 / San Yin Jiao (三阴交 SP6): Located 3 cun above the medial malleolus (the bony protrusion on the inner ankle), directly on the anterior border of the tibia. Press and massage for 2-3 minutes bilaterally, once or twice daily. This point is the intersection of the three yin channels and is powerful for tonifying Spleen Qi, regulating transformation and transportation, and calming the spirit.

Stomach 36 / Zusanli (足三里 ST36): Located 3 cun below the knee, specifically 3 cun below the ST35/Dubi point (which is directly below the kneecap), and approximately one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the prominent bone running down the front-outside of the shin). Press and massage for 2-3 minutes bilaterally daily, or use warm moxa (a warming herb stick held 1-2 cm above the skin without touching, for 5-10 minutes) if you tolerate warmth. This is the foundational tonification point for Qi and blood, supports immunity and Spleen function, and is considered one of the most powerful points for restoring Qi deficiency.

Heart 7 / Shen Men (神门 HT7): Located at the wrist crease on the pinky-side (ulnar) of your wrist, in the ulnar crease at the radial edge of the ulnar artery. Press and massage gently with your thumb for 2-3 minutes bilaterally, particularly in the evening before bed. This point calms the Heart-Spirit, reduces anxiety, promotes sleep, and addresses the emotional disturbance component of your pattern.

Yintang / Fourth Hall (印堂 EX-HN3): Located at the midpoint between the eyebrows, at the top of the bridge of the nose where the eyebrows meet. This is not on an official channel but is an empirical point of great value. Perform gentle circular massage with one finger for 1-2 minutes, particularly when stressed or anxious. This point calms the Spirit, reduces headache (if present), and has a settling effect on the nervous system.
exercise: Tai Chi or Qigong practice: 20-30 minutes daily, either as a formal class or via video instruction. These practices directly address Liver Qi Stagnation by training smooth, unobstructed flow of Qi through the body. They simultaneously reduce stress (addressing the root driver), calm the nervous system (reducing anxiety), and gently move the body without generating excess heat. This is the single most effective exercise modality for your pattern.

Gentle yoga with emphasis on forward folds and spinal twists: 20-30 minutes, 3-4 times per week. Poses that twist the torso (such as gentle spinal twists) and fold forward (child's pose, forward fold) mechanically release Liver Qi stagnation. Avoid hot yoga and intense cardio. Cool-water swimming (if available) is also excellent, as it moves Qi, cools upper-body heat, and is gentle on the Qi-deficient system.
recommendations.emotional_care: Your anxiety and inferiority complex are not separate from your skin condition—they are integral to it and will not resolve through topical skin treatments alone. As your Liver Qi begins to flow more smoothly and your Spleen Qi is tonified, you will naturally experience reduced anxiety and greater emotional resilience. However, active emotional work will accelerate this transformation and prevent relapse. Practice daily self-compassion: recognize that the skin condition has caused legitimate emotional pain, but it does not define your worth or capability. Consider working with a therapist or counselor experienced in psychosomatic conditions (skin-stress relationships are becoming increasingly recognized in conventional medicine as well). Join a support group for chronic skin conditions if possible, to reduce the sense of isolation. Practice the meditation 'I am worthy and my body is healing'—repeating this during acupoint massage and stress-management practice trains the nervous system toward safety and self-acceptance. Journaling about stress and emotional triggers can help identify the specific stressors maintaining your Liver Qi stagnation and allow you to address them proactively.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Free Constraint Powder (Xiao Yao San variant for Heat management)
ingredients: Bupleurum (柴胡 Chai Hu) 6g - soothes Liver Qi, primary regulator of stagnation
White Peony Root (白芍 Bai Shao) 10g - nourishes blood, softens Liver, reduces inflammation
Red Peony Root (赤芍 Chi Shao) 8g - moves blood and clears heat, addresses crimson plaques
White Atractylodes (白术 Bai Zhu, specifically Atractylodes macrocephala) 8g - strengthens Spleen, transforms dampness
Poria (茯苓 Fu Ling) 10g - transforms damp, supports Spleen Qi, calms spirit
Chinese Angelica Root (当归 Dang Gui) 6g - nourishes blood, supports Liver, gentle moistening action
Honey-fried Licorice (炙甘草 Zhi Gan Cao) 5g - tonifies Qi, harmonizes other herbs
Lophatherum (淡竹叶 Dan Zhu Ye) 6g - clears heat, calms Heart-Spirit, supports this pattern specifically
Mint (薄荷 Bo He) 2g - courses Liver Qi, opens pores, supports circulation
herbal_formulas.dosage: Decoct (simmer) in water: place herbs in a clay or stainless-steel pot, cover with 2 cups water, bring to boil then reduce heat and simmer for 30-40 minutes until liquid reduces to approximately 1 cup. Strain and drink warm, twice daily (morning and evening, 30 minutes before or after meals). Take for 4 weeks initially, then reassess with your practitioner. As symptoms improve, dosing may reduce to once daily. Total duration typically 8-12 weeks.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This formula directly addresses your complete pattern: Bupleurum, White Peony, and Mint soothe and regulate Liver Qi Stagnation; Bai Zhu, Fu Ling, and Gan Cao tonify Spleen Qi and support transformation; Red Peony and Lophatherum clear Damp-Heat and address the skin inflammation; Chinese Angelica nourishes blood and supports the Liver system. This is not a pure Damp-Heat formula (which would be too cold) nor a pure tonification formula (which would be too stagnating), but a balanced formula addressing the root deficiency while managing the excess manifestation. The formula is gentle enough for long-term use without side effects, though some patients experience a mild increase in thirst (due to the heat-clearing herbs) which resolves within 3-5 days of starting.

warning_signs: Sudden spread of rash to large areas of the body, or appearance of pustules, crusting, or oozing—these suggest secondary infection or acute inflammatory escalation requiring immediate dermatology evaluation

New onset of joint pain, swelling, or stiffness accompanying the skin condition—this raises concern for an underlying autoimmune condition (such as psoriasis vulgaris with arthropathic manifestations) requiring rheumatology assessment
Fever, swollen lymph nodes, or systemic illness symptoms—these require urgent medical evaluation to exclude infection, lymphoma, or systemic inflammatory disease
Suicidal thoughts or severe depression worsening despite herbal support—mental health crisis requiring immediate psychiatric evaluation and possible medication
Significant worsening of itching or plaques within the first week of herbal formula (suggesting an allergic reaction to one of the herbs)—discontinue formula and report to your TCM practitioner
contraindications: Do NOT use potent liver-heating formulas (such as Long Dan Xie Gan Tang or other bitter cold formulas containing Gentian Root) without practitioner supervision, as these will further deplete your Qi and may worsen the condition long-term
Do NOT use pure warming tonics (such as Korean red ginseng or Ephedra-containing formulas) as primary treatment, as these will aggravate the upper-body heat and fire up the inflammation

Do NOT attempt to 'cure the heat' with only topical steroids or pharmaceutical anti-inflammatory treatment, as this will suppress the manifestation without addressing the root Qi-Liver-Spleen dysfunction and will likely lead to relapse and possible steroid dependency

Do NOT stop herbal treatment abruptly after 2-3 weeks—many patients see initial improvement and stop too early; the root Qi deficiency requires 6-8 weeks minimum to stabilize, and stopping prematurely often results in relapse within weeks
precautions.special_notes: The proposed herbal formula contains no herbs known to interact with conventional psychiatric medications (SSRIs, SNRIs) or common medical treatments. However, if you are taking licorice-containing supplements or have hypertension, please inform your TCM practitioner before starting, as licorice in this formula (Gan Cao) is honey-fried and in modest dosage but can elevate blood pressure in susceptible individuals. The formula contains no immunosuppressants and is safe with typical dermatology care. If you develop new symptoms or the pattern changes significantly (for example, if lower-body symptoms develop or the plaques become purulent), inform your practitioner immediately as this may warrant formula adjustment. Women planning pregnancy should inform their TCM practitioner before continuing long-term, as some ingredients may need modification during conception and pregnancy (though this formula is generally safe).

follow_up.timeline: Reassess your condition after 2-3 weeks of consistent treatment (herbal formula + daily acupoint massage + daily stress-management practice). At this point, you should notice reduced anxiety, deeper sleep, and some reduction in itching intensity. At 4 weeks, schedule a follow-up consultation with your TCM practitioner to evaluate the response and potentially adjust the formula. Most patients with similar patterns see significant improvement by 6-8 weeks, with continued gradual improvement through 12 weeks. If no improvement is seen after 4 weeks, revisit the diagnosis and consider whether additional assessment (such as a conventional dermatology evaluation) is warranted.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1-2: You may notice slightly increased itching as the formula begins to move stagnant Qi (this is often a positive sign called 'healing crisis'), improved sleep quality, and early reduction in anxiety. Week 2-3: Itching should stabilize and begin to decrease; emotional irritability and stress reactivity should noticeably improve; skin plaques may remain red but feel less hot and intense. Week 4-6: Clear reduction in plaque extent and itching frequency; emotional mood should be noticeably lighter and more stable; dandruff should begin to diminish. Week 8-12: Significant fading of plaques (they may leave some residual discoloration that takes 4-6 weeks longer to resolve), anxiety substantially reduced, sleep excellent, and sense of well-being restored. The skin often continues to improve after the primary herbal course ends due to the restored underlying Qi circulation and stress resilience.
follow_up.next_steps: After 6-8 weeks of primary treatment, work with your TCM practitioner to decide on a maintenance approach: some patients benefit from continuing a gentler tonification formula (without the heat-clearing components) for another 4-8 weeks to fully stabilize the Qi and prevent relapse; others transition to dietary management and acupoint self-care combined with continued stress-management practice. Long-term prevention relies on maintaining daily stress-management practice (Tai Chi, meditation, or yoga), consistent sleep schedule, dietary alignment, and mindfulness of stress triggers. If stress escalates in the future (e.g., due to life changes or work pressure), return to regular acupoint massage immediately as a preventative measure to interrupt Liver Qi stagnation before it re-manifests as skin disease. Follow-up herbal support may be needed 1-2 times yearly during high-stress seasons or after major life events.

parsed.disclaimer: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) is a comprehensive system of medicine with its own diagnostic and therapeutic logic, but it is complementary to, not a replacement for, conventional medical care. The diagnosis and recommendations provided here are based on TCM principles and should not delay or replace any necessary conventional medical evaluation, particularly dermatological or psychiatric assessment if red-flag symptoms develop. A licensed TCM practitioner or acupuncturist should review and supervise your herbal formula before starting, particularly if you have other medical conditions, take other medications, or are pregnant. While the proposed modifications to your lifestyle and herbal support are based on well-established TCM patterns and are generally safe, individual responses vary. If you experience adverse reactions to the herbal formula or if your symptoms worsen despite treatment, discontinue and seek evaluation immediately. TCM works best as part of an integrated approach combining herbal medicine, acupoint therapy, lifestyle modification, and emotional/psychological support; no single intervention alone will likely resolve a one-year chronic condition.
